Nothing to complain about Mafia, this is objectively a masterpiece that came out in 2002. The game tells the story about a Taxi Driver, Tommy Angelo. Tommy, while working at night in the 1930s, stumbled across 2 gangsters from the Salieri's Family. Since that night, his life changed entirely.

[h1]Sound and Music:[/h1]
While playing Mafia, the player will completely dive in the atmosphere of the game: perfect sound and music experience (I'll talk more technically about sounds and music later in this review). I highly recommend playing the game with Stereo Headphones. Just as an example, during the "A Trip To The Country" mission, that thunderstorm effect really makes you feel like you're in the game during the whole chapter.

[h1]Story, dialogues, cutscenes and stuff:[/h1]
Great Story. The story is directly connected with Mafia 2's Story: a very important event that happens in Mafia 2 is part of Mafia 1, so I personally suggest playing both games (Mafia 1, then Mafia 2). The plot is interesting: A taxi driver, Tommy Angelo, will make an encounter that will change his life forever. I won't spoil anything because I'd really like you to play the game and "discover" the plot by yourself. Great dubbing and great acting (at least in Italy) that will really make the game look like a movie.

[h1]The importance of the Story:[/h1]
This game is not useless: it will also teach you the importance of life and the values of life, such as honor and friendship, and teach you the importance of making the right choices in life. This game will give you something to think about in your brain, I can guarantee.

[h1]Story Linearity:[/h1]
This is an interesting thing of Mafia: Some missions (I think 2 missions) have 2 possible endings. Also, you have more than 1 possible way to complete some missions. Also, there's the possibility that some missions will have optional objectives (usually Luca Bertone's secondary missions) and hidden secrets that will change the way to progress in the mission or give you hidden stuff.

[h1]Gameplay Linearity:[/h1]
This is another interesting stuff in Mafia: Some parts of the city are "meant to work that way", I'll explain it better: for example, when you start a specific mission, you'll likely encounter "that police car in that defined place" everytime. This is given by the power of the LS3D engine (Mafia's engine): developers had the power to manipulate the random seed in order to always generate the same random traffic combination for a specific mission. If this looks too complicated to you, please look for "Random Seed" on Google.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
The gameplay feels really good. Controls are oldschool and working really well if the game is played with Keyboard and Mouse (hey, this is how it's mean to be played, honestly, since you need to aim and stuff). I personally don't like some stuff in the shooting system, ie. you don't instantly shoot with your weapon and some NPCs shoot a countless amount of bullets if you hit them. The game still feels easy overall, nothing that a smart woman like Melody can't handle!

[h1]Graphics and Atmosphere:[/h1]
I've merged Graphics and Atmosphere here for a simple reason: the game is from 2002, which means that the graphics quality of Mafia won't amaze you that much, there are no excuses (I'll talk about graphics later in this review). Though, personally, even though I must admit that the graphics quality isn't that good for today's standards, I still feel the graphics and the atmosphere great and I still dive into the game whenever I play it.

[h1]Game Bugs:[/h1]
No gamebreaking bugs here. There are some minor issues not even worth mentioning. There's a very rare bug in the "Just for Relaxation" chapter in which the truck at the port may get stuck instead of driving out, you can fix it by just reloading the last savegame (the last savegame will spawn you right there, so there's no problem at all).

[h1]PC Exclusive: Free Ride Extreme:[/h1]
This is a PC Exclusive special gamemode. I won't spoil what it is, I'll just tell you that you'll spend a lot of time in it.

[h1]Problems, Solutions and Suggestions:[/h1]
Well, having Mafia on Steam is a great thing, but, sometimes, things aren't perfect.
[b]Missing music:[/b]
In the Steam version, some music is missing due to copyright issues. There's a fully-working community patch that can handle this problem, please search for it in the Steam Guides.
[b]Graphics Quality:[/b]
Make sure to run the configuration before booting up Mafia! Make sure to enable TrueColor textures and disable texture compression, also set everything on maximum quality.
[b]Audio bugs/issues:[/b]
The game expects very old audio hardware, thus enabling audio acceleration (such as EAX) will produce unexpected results. Make sure to enable software audio processing in the initial configuration tool and to disable the EAX feature (which is not required by the way, since software audio processing will process 3D audio by CPU). If you're still experiencing issues, please try changing your Audio Card frequency to 16-bit 44100 Hz or 16-bit 48000 Hz. 24-bit shouldn't affect anything, but give it a shot to change it if you're not sure.
[b]Graphics Glitches:[/b]
There are graphics glitches in shadows and reflections. This is easily fixable by installing a mod named "DX8 to DX9 Convertor", provided by the ENB Series author: there's a specific version for Mafia, the v0.0014. Install that by copying d3d8.dll and enbconvertor.ini to <Mafia install directory>\Mafia. Edit enbconvertor.ini so you don't load any proxy library (EnableProxyLibrary=0).
[b]Video Quality settings not saving:[/b]
Video Quality settings in the in-game menu will revert to default values once you quit the game. You need to go to Video Settings and set them to maximum everytime you boot the game, don't forget to do that!
[b]No Anisotropic filtering and crappy Antialiasing:[/b]
Use your NVIDIA/AMD/Intel Control Panel in order to improve application's antialiasing settings and force anisotropic filtering. This is really useful to improve graphics quality and fix graphics glitches caused by the in-game antialiasing!

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
In conclusion, you should really get this game: buy it and finish it. Don't skip cutscenes as they're really important in this game. You won't regret.

[h1]▶️Introduction[/h1]
As usual after my Mafia Definitive Edition review I would follow that up with the detailed review of the 2002 released game. Mafia was developed by 2K Czech and published by 2K. The game is a third person open world crime game taking place in a city called Lost Heaven which isn’t a real city but it does take many ideas of 1930s Chicago. As the name suggests, the main plot in the game is being part of the Mafia back in the 1930s.

Release Date : 28th August 2002

Last known update: Some months ago due to the licensed music.

[h1]🎩Small-talk:[/h1]
[i]How does Mafia 2002 play out in 2020?[/i]

[b]Smalltalk[/b]
Now as a Mafia fanboy I like to revisit one of my all-time favorite games from time to time and let me tell you that this masterpiece still feels somewhat modern despite being 18 years old. Sure the game is showing its age but compared to other all time great games it still feels modern, compare it to Deus Ex or perhaps GTA 3? Both games feel dated now despite being as old as Mafia, that only says a lot about the quality of this game.

[h1]🎮Gameplay:[/h1]

[b]Movement and shooting mechanics:[/b]
In this section we will see the biggest hint that this game came out in 2002, the movement is completely wonky and unresponsive. First of all you cannot even move your camera, this was a common design decision for 3rd person games of that era. So having a fixed viewing angle is a little annoying but another sight problem is the fact that you cannot see your players legs as the camera view displayer everything over his back. The actual movement is pretty basic as well but a lot slower compared to GTA games, that throws me to my biggest reasoning, the slow pace is the only major reason why as to why this game feels just a little old, sprinting wasn’t an option, fast vehicles weren’t either and just overall the game felt as if it was in slow-mo. Shooting weapons on the other hand felt rewarding, keep in mind you couldn’t control the recoil of the Tommy Gun as the game was designed like that so you would have to give some effort as far as recoil control goes. Mafia is one of the very few games that feel extremely rewarding yet challenging at the same time. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1330216886

[b]Driving:[/b]
Driving is by many considered as the weak point or Achilles heel of this masterpiece of a game, in my opinion driving is one of the many mechanics that give so much character to this game in the way it plays out. Vehicles do feel slow which by a lot of people is a negative but in all honesty, it is time correct and every car from the 1930s was extremely slow compared to what we got today, many people compare this game to the driving in GTA 3 or Vice City but people fail to realise that one game takes place in the 30s while the others in the 80s-90s-00s. Mafia 1 has such great driving details like the taillights, the wobble the suspensions make after suddenly turning, the weight pushing on the left side after doing a right hand turn, these are small details that make this game such a legend. Another misconception is the fact that the Formula 1 mission is basically a bad mission because of these mechanics, but once again I totally disagree, this is what gives purpose for this mission, not anybody can drive a race car, that’s just what it is, it feels rewarding to win against some 2002 racing game AI, impressive, isn’t it?

[b]Other aspects:[/b]
[*]City trains are totally usable and actually somewhat cool to experience.

[*]After completing the story you can play “Free Ride” which has many more missions for you.

[*]The progress bar while picklocking a vehicle is a very nice addition and I do wonder why this did not reappear in the Definitive Edition.
[/list]

[h1]🎭Story:[/h1]
Be aware, spoilers ahead!
 
Nothing much was changed in the Definitive Edition, actually more things got included. I will link the Mafia Story plus the additions here. [url=https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ylHkYwdoOIwrewqbHTjLHDzVYt5kiehqoCT9xPX8OXg/edit?usp=sharing]Complete Mafia 1 story[/url]

Now what additions did we get, as far as I remember, Sam was the guy that ordered Tommy to save his mistress/ Lover in the “Kill the Hotel manager” mission. In the 2002 release it was actually Tommy deciding to let her live.
Another addition was with Tommy’s wife Sarah, in the original game you had some very minor encounters with her leaving you to think that they were married while the Remake shows clear hints that this is a family.
Paulie also gets more depth as before the Bank Heist he explains to Tommy that he doesn’t want to lose his life without finding love or having a normal job, while in the original game you basically hear him out explaining how everything is going to go down.

Nearly a great story, sadly some holes appear.

[h1]🌇Graphics / Audio:[/h1]
For a 2002 game I have to admit that the face designs do look impressive.

Mafia is a 2002 open world action game, one of the earliest in the genre. Though it came out after Grand Theft Auto 3 and was frequently compared to it, it really set out to do something very different and deliver a very unique experience for the time.

Mafia takes place in the 1930s in a city called Lost Heaven. The storyline is equal parts the Godfather and Goodfellas. It's extremely long and extremely challenging, a few missions can take a dozen attempts to complete. This is probably the weakest part of the game, however the story is fairly good and keeps your attention so it's worth getting through to see the end.

The developers went to great effort to try and replicate the time period in almost a sim-like way. The police will stop you for speeding or running red lights. Cars accelerate very slowly and spin out very easily, it's often hard for one to even clear a hill. They went to great pains to reconstruct period friendly cars from the era and this really shows in the game. This was a decade prior to LA Noire doing much the same thing. Guns also have lots of recoil and the main automatic weapon you have access to controls like a rabid animal when you try and spray it. 

This is what makes Mafia very unique to me as a game. Most modern games that are set in different historical eras just treat it like an aesthetic or a skin. Mafia tries to be accurate even if it means it needs to inconveniance the player. And I wish more games tried to be more like Mafia and less like Grand Theft Auto 3.

Mafia probably had the misfortune of being released after Grand Theft Auto III, which meant that the game was inevitably compared to the cult sandbox game. But there is actually something else fundamental behind Mafia. it is more of a linear, story driven experience that trades chaotic sandbox freedom for narrative structure, atmosphere and immersion.

The story is arguably the centerpiece of the game. It spans several years and is told through a series of flashbacks as the main character, Tommy Angelo, recounts his life in the mafia family to a detective. This framing device helps the game cover a long stretch of time in a believable and paced way, with time jumps and changes in the city supporting the feeling of progression. Tommy is a more believable character: he's not a criminal by nature, but a regular taxi driver who is pulled into the world of organized crime by circumstance. The early missions highlight this, showing his everyday life and how it gradually falls apart, leaving him little choice but to join the Salieri family. It's a grounded and effective approach that makes the character feel more human and his decisions more understandable.

Despite having a large map, Mafia doesn't offer much in terms of free exploration or sandbox style content. Missions are tightly structured and follow a clear path from one point to the next, with little reason to stray off the beaten track. This becomes noticeable after a while: where in GTA III I could recall the layout of the city from memory because of all the time spent roaming around, Lost Heaven remained a vague collection of roads and landmarks. I mostly followed the mission markers, rarely wandering off. And yet, the city still feels like a real place.

Lost Heaven is carefully designed to reflect a 1930s American metropolis, complete with appropriate architecture, music, and everyday life. People go about their routines. Sometimes you see people park their cars and go for a walk. The city has also less forgiving rules: speed limits are enforced, cars need fuel, and the police will intervene if you break traffic laws or cause trouble. The presence of a larger countryside area, including places like a dam that you never actually visit in any mission, reinforces the idea that you're just one part of a bigger world. These details ground the experience in a way few games of its time attempted.

One of the most interesting aspects of the setting is how it evolves. Since the story takes place over several years, the city changes too. Construction sites you drive past in early missions may be completed later on. The cars in traffic are gradually replaced by newer models. These small details subtly reinforce the passage of time and give a sense of life beyond the immediate plot.

That being said, driving in Mafia is often not very exciting. The vehicles handle slowly and awkwardly, likely a result of trying to accurately depict the clunky cars of the era. This realism may not appeal to everyone, but it does serve the immersion. You're not expected to speed around corners or escape the police with ease. In fact, reckless driving will almost certainly get you arrested or worse. Where driving in a GTA title is part of the fun, here it's more of a controlled and cautious activity. It may not be thrilling, but it fits the tone of the game.

Gunfights in Mafia are similarly grounded. A few bullets can take you down, forcing you to approach shootouts carefully and tactically. The game lacks a formal cover system, but you can crouch and hide behind objects. Enemy AI isn't smart, but they tend to have good aim, which makes blind rushing a bad idea. You're limited in the number of weapons you can carry, with one larger firearm and a couple of pistols, which again contributes to the realism. The selection of weapons is decent, and though grenades and molotovs exist, they're rarely used and mostly forgettable. Overall, combat is serviceable but often frustrating, especially when paired with trial and error. It feels like the weakest part of the game and stands in contrast to the careful immersion established elsewhere. Still, it manages to offer some variety in scenarios and doesn't completely fall apart.

Where Mafia really shines is in its attention to small details. You can shoot out car tires and windows, and bullet holes remain visible on vehicles. Fuel leaks cause your gas to run out faster. Civilians may sometimes pick up guns from fallen enemies and fight back.

There is a freeride mode, but without missions or real objectives, it quickly feels empty. The city is visually detailed, but outside of the main story, there's little to engage with. The "Freeride Extreme" mode offers absurd challenges and unlocks fantasy style cars, some of which have enhanced performance. But even these can feel odd, as the game's driving mechanics were never built to support high speed vehicles.

When it was released, Mafia didn't get universal praise. It was often dismissed as just another GTA clone, judged by its surface similarities rather than its actual goals. But in reality, it shares more with simulation games. The slow driving, the deadly shootouts, the limited freedom all of it is part of a deliberate illusion. Mafia isn't trying about playground of chaos but about a immersive and realistic story.

It's not perfect, so don't expect an open world with lots of content or entertaining activities. The gameplay also sucks at some points. But the narrative and story are great.

Mafia used to be my favourite game in 2006. I decided to replay Mafia a couple of days ago as it'd been 15 years since I last (and first) played it. The game hasn't aged considerably and to my mind creates the same distinct impression as it did in the past. I enjoyed the playthrough again. 

The major pros of the game, apart from the plot, are the old school music, authentic cars and characters' personalities. Lonnie Johnson, The Mills Brothers, Django Reinhardt have been some of my favourite musicians for many years, and it was Mafia that introduced me to them. 

The major cons of the game are the character controls and in-game camera. Aiming, shooting and especially fighting are clunky as hell. I wish they had made a first-person view and a dodge system. Free Ride Extreme is also ludicrous and dull. It's just absurd. 

All in all, Mafia manages to retain its tense and gripping atmosphere of the 30s.

On the positive side, the game delivers a compelling narrative, supported by gorgeous cinematics and an atmospheric soundtrack that nails the mood at every turn. The story moments are memorable, and the presentation does a fantastic job of drawing you into the world. Unfortunately, the actual gameplay doesn’t quite live up to that standard. The on-foot controls feel clunky and unresponsive, making basic movement and combat more of a chore than they should be. This is compounded by frustrating gameplay elements poorly designed encounters, awkward mechanics, and pacing issues that often break immersion. The result is a constant tug-of-war between moments of brilliance and moments of irritation: a game that shines when it leans into its story and atmosphere but stumbles whenever it asks you to take direct control.

As a cinema-lover (I am reluctant to call myself a cinephile though, since I don't watch that many films), I am often disappointed with stories in games. Mafia (2002) is a true masterpiece. The game’s intro is simply stunning  the music, the city reveal, and the way it introduces you to the world immediately immerse you in the 1930s. Nostalgic tunes and carefully designed streets full of classic cars, trams, subways, and pedestrians make the city feel alive.

The story takes place in 1930s America  during Prohibition, with a corrupt police force and high-ranking officials involved in mafia dealings. We follow Tommy Angelo, a taxi driver drawn into the world of the mob. His transformation from an ordinary man into a member of the Salieri family shows how thin the line is between loyalty and betrayal. Every decision carries consequences, and the world he lives in doesn’t forgive mistakes. Relationships with characters like Paulie and Sam add authenticity and depth to the story.

Each mission is its own story  from stealthy hits and robberies to quiet surveillance and small favors for the family. The unforgettable race tests both patience and skill. Exploring the city is pure joy  during missions or in free-roam mode, you could travel not just by car but also by tram and subway, which was rare in games back then. Every street, every passerby, every detail makes Lost Heaven feel like a living, breathing city. Driving vintage cars and listening to period music really makes you feel the era. Exploring the city, riding the subway, passing pedestrians  it all creates an extraordinary sense of life in pre-war America.

What sets Mafia apart from other gangster games is its style  gritty, cinematic, and mature. It’s not just about action  it’s a story about ambition, loyalty, betrayal, and the price one pays. The plot isn’t afraid to slow down for emotional impact. Each scene carries weight, and the ending stays with you long after.

For me personally, this is more than a game  it’s a real journey through time. Sometimes moving, sometimes tense, full of passion and details that make you want to return to it. Mafia is a vivid, atmospheric story where every corner of the city and every note of music build a unique world. This is a game that offers something many modern titles can’t – a true soul and emotions that stay with you long after you’ve finished.

Important notes before I start the review: For the best experience, I highly suggest installing the Mafia Restore Original Music mod. This will add all of the licensed music that was removed due to copyright. This music adds more atmosphere to the game and some more excitement to the action sequences. The Unlimited Draw Distance mod: https://www.nexusmods.com/mafia/mods/3/?tab=description (IMPORTANT: If you're going to use this mod, then be sure to go into the Mafia file directory, then into the "MISSIONS" folder that you got from installing the mod, then delete the "MISE20-GALERY" file. This will fix a bizarre skybox problem in the art gallery level). (Mod effects are explained in the "Description" tab of the Nexus Mods page).

The Widescreen Fix mod: https://www.nexusmods.com/mafia/mods/2/ (effects are also explained in the "Description" tab of the Nexus Mods page).

ENBSeries DX8 to DX9 Convertor: http://enbdev.com/convertor_dx8_dx9_v0014.htm (this will fix flickering shadows and blood). 

Borderless Gaming: https://sourceforge.net/projects/borderless-gaming.mirror/ (use this if you're experiencing issues in fullscreen such as outline flashes and low frame rate). 

Well, that's the technical stuff out of the way. Now, let's begin! 

Mafia is a 2002 open world third-person shooter set during the 1930's in a fictional city called Lost Heaven. You play as Tommy Angelo, an innocent cab driver unexpectedly thrust into the world of the Mob. After becoming a member of the Salieri crime family, Tommy must undertake various tasks such as securing a shipment of whiskey, winning a race that the Don bet a lot of money in, saving your friend in a motel occupied by ruthless gangsters, killing a politician with ties to the enemy Mafia etc. Speaking of the enemy Mafia, the Morello crime family is a dangerous foe that Tommy now has to look out for and eventually help to destroy. While completing all these tasks, you can also explore the city of Lost Heaven, taking in the atmosphere of bustling streets, good music, and admiring lots of Depression-era architecture. As well as that, you can do subquests that will help you unlock new cars to use later in the game. If this short summary interests you, then you'll be pleased to know that there's more about this game that may interest you. 

One aspect of Mafia that I think is praiseworthy is the gameplay. The combat, for instance, was a lot of fun for me. I liked mowing down enemies with a Tommy gun, blasting them up close with a shotgun, picking them off at a distance with a Springfield rifle etc. I also enjoyed the driving as well as the missions in general that I feel were decently well designed, managing to be exciting as well as compelling (albeit quite frustrating at times, especially the subquests). The melee combat was alright, but not great (more on that later). I also think that the enemy AI was quite decent and put up a genuine challenge: Enemies took cover, rolled to avoid my gunfire, called me out and insulted me etc. The destruction physics of the cars was also a nice addition, with headlights, windshields, tires, wheels etc. being destroyed and/or falling off when enough damage was done to them. This may be a small detail but a noteworthy one regardless. I feel I should also mention the Free Ride mode, offering you the choice of exploring the city of Lost Heaven however much you want with no campaign missions to worry about. You can drive around, steal cars, run over pedestrians, get into gunfights with the cops etc. So think of it as a Great Depression-era GTA game. There's also the Free Ride Extreme mode where there are no cops, some ramps, and crazy missions to beat (e.g. chasing a UFO, chasing and killing a man with super speed, saving a woman from a sea monster etc.).

Another aspect of Mafia I should praise is the story. I loved following Tommy's journey in the Mafia, seeing his whole world turn upside down was thrilling as well as fascinating. The way the story was told was great too, with well-animated (for the time) cutscenes being used for mission briefings as well as narrated segments and important scenes between Tommy and a detective in a restaurant that show up throughout the game, as if to hint to the player that the story is being told by Tommy himself. The competent voice acting also added to the story, with each character having a suitable voice and therefore helping to immerse you further into the world of Mafia. I should also mention that the dialogue was quite good too. 

One more positive thing I'd like to touch on is the atmosphere. The visuals, although dated, still managed to create many splendid urban environments for me to appreciate, not to mention the excellent soundtrack that includes not only orchestral music but also brilliant classics from artists such as Django Reinhardt, The Mills Brothers, Latcho Drom and more. Hearing different songs depending on what part of the city I was in certainly was delightful, as well as hearing adrenaline-fuelling accordion music in a couple of intense chase missions. That's really all I can say about the atmosphere. It's great. 

Now I think would be a good time to talk about the negatives of this game. The first I can think of is that some of the textures would flicker. Even after I installed the ENB Convertor I still had this problem, which was a shame since the flickering textures were rather distracting at times. Another negative I can think of is that, while driving, I would occasionally hear weird audio pops and clicks, especially when honking the horn of the car I was in. I tried fixing this but didn't manage to find a proper fix. Another complaint I have is about the melee combat which I feel was mediocre (especially in comparison to the gunplay). It just felt awkward (especially in the "Better Get Used to It" mission). One other negative aspect of this game for me was how frustrating some of the quests were. Quite a few of the subquests and many of the Free Ride Extreme mode missions were particularly infuriating. I also noticed that the countryside landscapes were hideous and that some areas of the game's world map looked odd and unfinished (e.g. the large floating sheet of grass with some trees on it, an island with a huge hole on the side of it etc.) but to be fair, I probably only noticed this because I was using the Unlimited Draw Distance Mod. Still, I would've preferred for the world map to not be so shoddy in certain places. Another flaw I encountered were the occasional bugs. For example, in the "Just For Relaxation" mission, I had to follow this truck leaving the docks, but sometimes the truck wouldn't even leave, meaning I had to reload my save in order for the mission to actually work properly. Later in that mission there was a task where I had to stack some crates with two NPCs, but the mission could only continue if all the crates were neatly stacked (something only the two NPCs could do), so because I stacked the last crate just as the two NPCs were leaving and since I couldn't ask them to stack the crates again, I ended up having to reload my save and do that part all over again (this time letting the NPCs do nearly all of the work). To put it lightly, this was mildly infuriating. I should also mention the fact that the frame rate was much lower during the nighttime and evening sections than in the usual daytime sections of the game and that the option for subtitles is, strangely enough, hidden away in an additional options menu (called "Others") in the "Controls" menu. Other than that, I don't really have much else to complain about. 

So to conclude: Mafia is an enjoyable game that tells an exciting tale of an innocent man being thrust into the ugly world of organised crime. It may not be perfect, but what game is? 

Final verdict: 6.8/10 "Mr. Salieri sends his regards."

Oh boy where do I even start, "Mafia" is an old classic, a very underrated game by today's standards. I remember playing this game when i was in grade school, much later in 2011 I bought this game on Steam too and I have never actually wrote a review for this game. 
Reading through other reviews by people, the media and even newer "retro" reviews I was glad that people do still remember this great game even after more than 16 years since it was released. On the other hand I was annoyed a bit that people still try to compare "Mafia" to the "Grand Theft Auto" series which just blows my mind, this game isn't GTA and it was never meant to be a "GTA" game. Just because there is a semi-open world with a bit of driving involved, a character that you control in 3rd person doesn't mean it's automatically a "GTA" clone.

"Mafia" is a linear game that is trying to show and tell a realistic story about organized crime back in the 1930s and sure it does it very well. The summary of the game's story is that you are Thomas Angelo, a normal guy trying to make a living by driving a Taxi for a respectable company. One day you are caught up with two mobsters at the wrong place and wrong time, forced to help these mobsters get away from some other guys. When you get these men back to their safe location at the "Salieri's Bar", they show you appreciation from their Don because you helped them get away. They even offered Tommy a job if he is willing to work for them because they appreciate a guy that helped them. Later on Tommy will get jumped by the other mobsters from the rival family who were chasing the guys Tommy just saved a day before. Tommy successfully escapes from these mobsters back to the Salieri's bar where he dropped off Salieri's guys just a day before. This is how the story starts for Thomas Angelo, a new guy, just joined the Salieri family because he was kind of forced to get help from them. After these events the game's story continues to show Thomas Angelo as he rises through the ranks of organized crime. 
For a game this old it holds up really good even after 16 years, obviously there are minor bugs and glitches here and there but it's not like games nowadays don't have any, right? 
This game is a classic and in my opinion the best work that "Illusion Softworks" did in this genre of games, there's other good games that portray a realistic image of organized crime back in the 1930s but this game tops them all off.
To conclude my review, in my opinion this game is a masterpiece that told a realistic story and I don't think any new game in the coming years will ever come this close to being this good as "Mafia" is.

It's probably the best mafia game ever but stay away. I got it on sale but I wouldn't get it even if free: the music missing from the Steam version, parts of the dialogue missing, very buggy voices and sounds. It's shameful what they did to the game.

Despite the enormous bloodshed, Mafia is ultimately a very charming game. You really feel like a part of the Salieri family, as you work together with your buddies to get things done. Tommy is a relatable character, because he doesn't start out as a criminal. It kinda happened to him, though at the same time it was his own choice. Many times, the story will make you ask the question "Is it worth it?"

The developers put in a lot of effort in bringing the game to life. The voice acting is above average for its time, each character has their own gestures and body language. Most interesting subtle detail is, every time you go to Vincenzo he's always doing something else, and walks to his table once you enter. It takes some extra time to get to business, but it gives you this sense that he's a real person doing his own stuff when you're not there.
There are also traffic rules. You can get fined if you run the red traffic light, even though it doesn't mean anything since there's not really money in the game. I think this is an interesting mechanic, because it makes the traffic lights real, rather than just props.

The 1930's are iconic, cute cars with tiny chassis, gunmen wearing suits and hats, iconic weapons like the Colt 1911 and Thompson submachine gun.

I wish public transport was a bigger part of the story, because it was a lot of fun to take the train and see the city from a different perspective, and it was also nice that I didn't have to drive for once.
Speaking of driving, Mafia has surprisingly good driving mechanics, though it's a little less surprising once you know that Mafia was originally conceived as a racing game.
But there are 2 small problems I have: 
1. it switches back to automatic transmission every time you reload a checkpoint. so I have to manually switch it back to manual gearing. at some point I just gave up.
2. there's no cockpit view. most of the time you're using the bird's eye camera, which feels less immersive, and also very slow. It doesn't help that there's a speed limit of 40 mph, and police will chase you if they see you go 41 mph or more. Luckily it's often easy to lose the cops. And police cars show up on the radar so you can adjust speed accordingly.

The shooting in this game feels very awkward by modern standards. There is a lot of recoil, that takes a long time to recover. But this is compensated by the awkward AI that very rarely hits you. The typical hitman has an accuracy of 10% or so. They also don't really know how to be aggressive, and you can often just shoot their arm while they can't see you. Even so, I've died a lot of times. There's not many health packs around, so you have to do everything to not get lose HP.

The game is a little buggy, but nothing too game-breaking. At one point I had a kneeling cop floating in the air at the airport. Very random.

All in all, a very impressive game and story. The boat mission was my favorite.
It's cool they have a Chinatown, even though there's not much there.
The biggest downside is that you can't look down on the city from Oak Hill. It just looks like an ocean.
That's why I can't wait to revisit Mafia in the Definitive Edition.

The police system is overly aggressive and often gets in the way of completing missions such that anything involving long car chases is down to chance that you don't run across a squad car. It makes timed mission jaunts through the city a chore. I honestly wish you could just turn it off because it pads the game out unnecessarily and not in a fun way. You can't even enjoy all the fancy fast cars you acquire because you're stuck doing a pedestrian 40 mph to avoid having yourself be stopped every 500 feet or rammed by magic police cars.

Similarly, the gunplay in this game is very uninspiring, and later missions are just goonhunts where you gamble on whether or not you will have enough health to absorb the shots that will be sent your way, - And they WILL hit! Shotgun enemies have laser-focused accuracy. - especially in the harbor mission where your character will start off a shootout with an UNLOADED WEAPON, guaranteeing that you will absorb at least 4 health damage minimum right off the bat as you wait for Tommy to fumble with his Colt 1911 while being shot at by the first enemy goon.

Thankfully you can disable the stupid 'tuck and roll' feature which makes gunfights far less frustrating than when Tommy decides you tapped A or D too quick to strafe and dives out of cover.

As far as missions go, bugs are more frequent than I remember them being, and certain missions will just require cheese to avoid the broken parts - Such as when the goons come out of the restaurant anyway while you're batting their cars, or when the goons putting a hit on Salieri at Pepe's straight-up phase-shift through the walls to blast you away. If you try to do the mission the 'correct' way, the game bugs out and punishes you anyway.

I could forgive everything else, as frustrating as it is, BUT the ONE THING that finally broke the camel's back is Creme de la Creme, one of the final missions. This mission is straight-up broken, no hyperbole. If you're unfortunate enough to have Morello's car turn into the airport, just repeat the countryside car chase section until he decides to go past the airport to the bridge. You can dump 3 full drums of Thompson bullets into the airplane's engines till they explode and watch the plane's health drop to zero, only to have the mission still deem it wasn't enough TO ACTUALLY FULFILL THE SUCCESS CONDITIONS OF THE MISSION, AND THE MISSION STILL FAILS ANYWAY. Genuinely broken.

Mafia: City of Lost Heaven is an open world action crime game and “hot dame” simulator developed by Illusion Softworks, a studio that was established in Brno located in the Czech Republic in 1997 and whose work up until release mainly included the Hidden & Dangerous tactical shooter series. However, aside from that, the actual development of the original Mafia had started in 1998, consisting of a team of five people or so and was originally a game called “Gangster”. It would initially use the engine of the Hidden & Dangerous series before the actual development of the game would be moved to the LS3D Engine, an engine that would mainly be used by lower budget studios to make games like Chameleon, more Armed and Dangerous games and Wings of War. This change would lead to development for the game taking an extra two years or so, with two directors coming to the forefront: Daniel Vavra and Petr Vochozka, the former of which I have more information on in the long run. Vavra was also the main writer for the game, having watched classics like The Godfather and Goodfellas and wanting to pay homage to movies like this in the form of a realistic video game with melancholic aspirations. Some concepts that were in development before being cut included a multiplayer mode, a racing menu as well as a body grabbing system to move around corpses you killed (perhaps for stealth reasons). Originally the team was around five people, though over the years it would grow to about twenty to forty people depending on the sources you pull from around the time of the release. How were the reviews for the game? First I’ll go over my feelings on it before following up on that.

For most of review, links included: https://backloggd.com/u/gamemast15r/review/3354509/

What’s there to say on the gameplay? I enjoy it a lot, but I can also understand how people would feel about it if they didn’t like it. I’ll start first on this with the combat/camera, as it’s very much an older game and it does things differently than the rest of the series. You’ll follow right behind Tommy at all times even outside of combat, the camera moving in the same direction that Tommy himself moves so you can’t exactly look around your surroundings like that. There’s no cover system so you can’t just hide behind a wall and shoot your gun wildly, instead you’ll need to crouch (to focus your aim better) and pop in and out left or right and shoot in order to kill someone unless you wanna go up for the kill. You have a health bar that goes up to 100 that sits in the lower left hand side of the screen that you’ll need to refill with first aid stations that don’t always make themselves obvious and are kind of few and far between depending on the mission. You will die really easily if you’re not careful, whether it’s getting unloaded on by a Tommy Gun or given a shotgun jumpscare that messes with me EVERYTIME. Actual checkpoints can have you replaying decent sections of a mission if you die. With everything that I listed feeling kind of archaic and annoying, then why do I like it so much? Maybe it’s a nostalgia thing but even despite my meh experience playing the Playstation 2 port, it just works well and I never really had an issue with it for the most part. I never had an issue with the actual combat or realism, and the truth is I only really felt hard pressed in terms of difficulty towards the last mission of the game or so just due to them introducing grenade throws. The actual gunplay itself feels fantastic between the various weapons, the feedback these weapons give, the satisfaction of putting down rival mobsters. Melee combat? So-so for the most part, as using your fists looks cool and sounds satisfying but you can also just kind of take a while to knock a guy out or you can get into a loop of getting knocked out. I honestly felt like combat sections were some of my favorite missions in the game, like the Italian Restaurant Ambush or The Farm. I feel like since there isn’t much else I can say here, I want to get into Mission Structure as this is where I feel like a lot of the focus on gameplay actually goes.

Before I start I want to say that the game definitely focuses on a hyper realism and can be considered frustrating for those who aren’t used to older styled gameplay. I love it however as the missions itself remained vary, and while there are some long checkpoints and I never really enjoyed driving across the entire city again because some goons murdered me or police got a hate b o n er on me for speeding, I always just kind of took it in stride and had a laugh because I found myself genuinely enjoying the game. It doesn’t feel like just nostalgia but it feels like that and meeting the game on it’s same expectations, though I’ll admit I went in kind of being scared of it because of how “realistic” it was. Another thing I really enjoy? The details, some that you wouldn’t really know about unless you kind of explored or went off the beaten path a bit, though it isn’t that crazy. For example, when chasing Morello he has four separate ways he can die with three of them providing their own cutscenes and which one plays is kind of random; shooting down his airplane, crashing him off a bridge, stopping just before the bridge and engaging in a shootout (no cutscene) or somehow driving well enough to stay right next to him for a bit during the chase so the others can wipe him out before he gets to the countryside. This level of detail? Amazing. The Prison Sniper Job? Kill the construction worker near the manhole and dump him into it and you won’t have to worry bout cops later. The game doesn’t tell you this stuff but it’s pretty damn cool to learn about this sort of stuff, and as such I’ll leave a Steam guide in the links (or in the Backlogg’d page links) for you to check out but it’s seriously cool that it’s open ended how to approach situations sometimes and I wish they kept that for later entries in the franchise. One of my favorite details actually has to do with getting rid of the wanted car for Lucas by the lighthouse; most people would park it by the edge of the cliff before grabbing another car and then pushing it in. Put it in Neutral and get out of the car and bam it’s in the ocean! Though this brings up another section: driving.

Zamanında hepimiz Godfather gibi kült mafya konulu yapımları izleyip hayran kaldık. Bu tür yapımlar, çoğumuzun aklında romantize edilen bir suç dünyası yaratmıştır: sadakat, güç, ihanet ve stratejilerle dolu bir dünya. Eğer siz de bu karanlık ve entrikalarla dolu atmosferin bir parçası olmak, mafya-vari bir dünyanın içerisinde birinci elden rol almak isterseniz, size önerebileceğim yegâne yapımlardan biri tam karşınızda duruyor. Bu yapım, sizi adeta 20. yüzyılın ortalarındaki klasik suç örgütlerinin içerisine çekiyor ve bir mafya üyesi olarak yükselişinizi deneyimlemenizi sağlıyor.

Grafikler, günümüz standartlarına göre belki göz kamaştırıcı değil, ancak atmosferi başarıyla yansıttığını söyleyebilirim. Şehir tasarımları, karakter modelleri ve dönemine uygun detaylarla dolu çevreler oyunun genel atmosferine katkı sağlıyor. Özellikle gece vakti şehirde dolaşırken ışıklandırmalar ve sis efekti gibi ince detaylar, oyuncuyu gerçekten o dünyaya ait hissettirebiliyor. Grafikler yeterli düzeyde olsa da, kimi oyuncuların daha modern görsellik beklentisi içinde olabileceğini göz önünde bulundurmak gerek. Yine de bu yapımın asıl gücü, atmosfer yaratmada ve sizi hikâyenin içine çekmede yatıyor.

Mekanikler ise ne yazık ki grafiklerin aksine biraz can sıkıcı olabilir. Kontroller bazen hantal hissettirebiliyor ve aksiyon anlarında beklenmedik hatalar yaşayabiliyorsunuz. Ancak bu kusurları, eğer mafya temalı yapımlara ilgi duyuyorsanız, göz ardı etmeniz pekâlâ mümkün. Oyunun sunduğu görev çeşitliliği ve ilerledikçe açılan hikâye öğeleri, mekaniksel eksikliklerini bir nebze de olsa affettiriyor. Ayrıca, mafya dünyasının katı kuralları ve hiyerarşisine uygun olarak ilerleyen olay örgüsü, stratejik düşünmeyi ve dikkatli kararlar almayı gerektiriyor. Bu da oyuncuya farklı bir derinlik sunuyor ve adeta bir suç lordu olmanın sorumluluklarını hissettiriyor.

Sonuç olarak, eğer bu tür oyunlar ilginizi çekiyorsa, kütüphanenize eklemenizi ve kesinlikle denemenizi tavsiye ederim. Eksikliklerine rağmen sunduğu atmosfer, hikâye derinliği ve klasik mafya yapımlarına olan saygısı ile sizi içine çekeceğine eminim. Oyun dünyasında geçireceğiniz her dakika, sizi daha fazla suç dünyasının içine sürükleyecek ve hikâyenin gidişatına dair merakınızı arttıracaktır. Hazır olun; bu yapımda bir mafya babası olmak sandığınız kadar kolay olmayabilir, ancak kesinlikle unutulmaz bir deneyim olacaktır.

[h1] Still one of the greatest games of all time, even after 20 years of being made. What The Godfather is for movies, Mafia is for video games [/h1]

The realism of this game is unmatched by most of the games in the genre:
- Cars running out of gas (even quicker if the gas tank gets shot) and gas stations with an actual purpose other than blowing up
- Realistic physical damage/scratches to cars
- Blinkers when turning
- Manual transmission (including the neutral gear)
- Easy to get shot down by bullets if you play like a dummy
- Running red lights and speeding gets you chased by the cops
- Car parts falling off and windows shattering, etc.... 

It's the little things that all add up to bring you a sense of realism that a lot of newer games fail to do, including the new remake of this game that I personally did not end up liking.

The good old music of the era, which is not provided by downloading the game from Steam by the way, but can be easily patched by downloading a library from the internet.

The story, the characters, the city, the car chases, the shootouts... One of a kind experience. It even has an addition of Free Ride (roam) and Free Ride Extreme, where you can complete crazy missions to get crazy cars, just for fun.

A must play.

This game holds such a big place in my heart. It used to be my safe haven during a difficult period in my teenage years. Specifically, I adored the taxi missions, I found comfort in them. It warmed my heart to just drive these old cars around the city of Lost Heaven.
I also love that progressing into the story feels rewarding because you gradually get more powerful cars, starting with the ones that can barely move (saying this lovingly). Plus, the driving physics here still beat those in many modern games. Finishing that notorious racing mission feels like defeating prime Radahn or idk what else.
The characters, they are so memorable that it took me a long while to get used to the ones in the remake. Although to me, the remake turned out to be just as good as the og. 
The story in its turn is so good that I've never ever skipped any of the cutscenes because experiencing them feels like reading beautiful chapters of a good book.

Incredible game, great story, honestly far more impressive than GTA III ever was.
